summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court exceeds its jurisdiction if it transfers legal custody of a child from a parent to the county department at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing; at that stage the court may only continue shelter or release the child, and a temporary protective custody order reaches physical custody only.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Colorado case on the limits of emergency protective custody: 72 hours maximum, physical custody only, with a shelter hearing within 48 hours.
key_cases.quote: We will not infer from statutory silence a jurisdictional grant to a juvenile court to sever legal custody from a natural parent at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing.

key_cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that procuring an ex parte child custody order through distortion, misrepresentation and omission, and in retaliation for a parent's retaining counsel, violated clearly established Fourth, First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: It reads C.R.S. § 19-3-405(2)(a) as permitting temporary protective custody only on a belief that remaining would endanger the child's life or health in the reasonably foreseeable future.
key_cases.quote: it was clearly established law that, except in extraordinary circumstances, a parent has a liberty interest in familial association and privacy that cannot be violated without adequate pre-deprivation procedures.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit adopted a reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removal, holding that officials may remove a child without prior notice and hearing only on reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the child's safety and must then provide a prompt post-removal hearing, and found the defendants entitled to qualified immunity on these facts.
key_cases.relevance: This is the governing Tenth Circuit standard for taking a child into protective custody without a court order.
key_cases.quote: even in these instances in which emergency removal is justified, the state must afford the parents a prompt post-removal hearing.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed a grant of qualified immunity, holding that the alleged coercive detention of a teenager at school by a social services official and a deputy, to compel her to change her residence, stated a violation of her clearly established Fourth Amendment right to be free from unreasonable seizure.
key_cases.relevance: Taking physical control of a child outside the home is a seizure that must be justified, not an administrative act.
key_cases.quote: the prohibition against unreasonable seizures extends to civil, as well as criminal, investigations by the government.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that UCCJEA temporary emergency jurisdiction is limited to abandoned children and to emergencies of mistreatment or abuse, that the juvenile court therefore lacked that jurisdiction when it terminated parental rights and the termination judgment was properly vacated, but that the division erred in directing contact with an Arkansas court without first analysing whether Arkansas had home-state jurisdiction on the date of the termination order.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency jurisdiction over a child present in Colorado but belonging to another state's courts exists only for abandonment or an actual ongoing emergency of mistreatment or abuse, which bounds the state's authority when it takes such a child into protective custody.
key_cases.quote: we hold that UCCJEA temporary emergency jurisdiction exists only to protect abandoned children or to prevent mistreatment or abuse in emergencies

mandatory_reporters: Enumerated professionals only — Colorado is not a universal-reporter state — Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-304(2) (C.R.S. 2024); any other person may report voluntarily under § 19-3-304(3)
Physicians and surgeons, including physicians in training
Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses
Hospital personnel engaged in the admission, care, or treatment of patients
Public or private school officials and employees
Social workers and workers in any facility or agency licensed or certified by the state
Commercial film and photographic print processors
Clergy members (not for information learned in a communication privileged under Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-90-107(1)(c))
Workers in the state department of human services
Officers and agents of the state bureau of animal protection, and animal control officers
Educators providing services through the federal WIC program
Directors, coaches, assistant coaches, and athletic program personnel employed by a private sports organization or program
Registered psychologist, marriage and family therapist, and licensed professional counselor candidates
Officials and employees of a county department of health or of human or social services
Employees of the department of early childhood
